title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness: the preregistered hypotheses H1/H2 about generator/repair comparative performance were preregistered but remain unobserved under the shared_initial_candidate execution semantics. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces) that: (i) the prompts sent to the model did not leak canonical reference answers (see provider_call artifacts and task manifest entries), and (ii) the repair subsystem was available per the preregistration but not triggered (repair_applied = false across per‑task scoring traces).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural approaches are common: translation‑first pipelines that restrict generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solvers, and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair. Prior literature emphasizes both deterministic guarantees and LLM‑driven flexibility, but direct, preregistered comparisons that produce artifactized per‑task validator traces are rare.

This study's preregistered head‑to‑head question was: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation: reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), the generator (gpt‑5‑mini), the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

A decisive preregistered design choice was shared_initial_candidate semantics: each paired task used a single LLM candidate generated once and supplied identically to both architectures. This choice intentionally removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand and therefore restricts the measured estimand to validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates. The preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 (comparing architecture performance under independent generation/repair) were therefore preregistered but unobserved under the executed shared_candidate semantics; the present paper makes that restriction explicit and documents the concrete artifacts that demonstrate both the shared‑candidate orchestration and the reasons repairs were not invoked.
sections.related_work: Two research traditions frame our contribution and motivate the experimental axes used in this study: (1) formal translation and verification systems that prioritize deterministic guarantees (e.g., SymNet and follow‑on translation/verification work) and (2) LLM‑driven agentic NetOps that emphasize flexible generation and iterative repair. Formal translation→verification work uses constrained DSLs and solver/verification feedback to provide acceptance/counterexample outputs and tends to exhibit low generator variance due to restricted output surfaces. LLM‑centric work instruments generate→validate→repair loops, measures repair coverage and transient unsafe proposals, and typically compares independent generator draws per arm. Our preregistered shared_candidate design sits orthogonally to independent‑generation comparisons: it isolates downstream acceptance behavior (validator‑parity) when upstream candidates are identical, a useful operational check when validating new validators/orchestrators.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and execution contract. The preregistration CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 (archived) fixed the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, maximum_model_calls = 240, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The execution adapter honored these constraints and archived the execution manifest.

Task generation and contamination controls. Confirmatory tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each manifest entry (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) contains: intent text, canonical reference answer, initial and expected final states, required safe sequences, and difficulty metadata. To rule out prompt/response contamination, provider‑call traces were archived for every shared generation and are the primary evidence of the exact prompts sent to the model (see execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000002-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000003-shared-initial.json). The execution accounting recorded model_calls_used = 120 (one independent hosted model call per paired task) and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json), demonstrating explicit execution isolation and no reused cached candidate across pairs or conditions.

What the provider_call artifacts and manifest entries show (artifact‑grounded). The task manifest entries archived alongside provider calls separate the task intent from the canonical reference answer (task manifest: execution/task_manifest.jsonl contains payload.intent and reference_answer fields for each task). The provider_call artifacts referenced above record the actual prompt delivered to the hosted model; inspection of those provider_call files (archived at execution/provider_calls/*) confirms that prompts included the task intent and constraints but did not contain the canonical reference answer used by the deterministic validator. These archived provider_call files are the primary artifact that rules out inadvertent leakage of the canonical reference into the prompt.

Generation, shared candidate semantics, and validator instrumentation. Orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: for each paired task the system invoked the hosted model once and supplied the identical textual candidate to both downstream arms. Execution accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json) records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion and ordering checks (make‑before‑break; shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and emits validation_after.valid (boolean). Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000XXX-*.json) record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags; these files are the canonical evidence for per‑task decisions.

Repair subsystem availability (preregistration vs invocation). The preregistration allowed bounded repairs (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) and included repair tracing fields in the scoring schema. In the executed artifacts the repair subsystem was available in orchestration (per preregistration/execution adapter contract) but not invoked: per‑task scoring traces contain repair_applied: false and repair_provider_trace_path: null for all episodes (examples below). Thus secondary estimands about repair coverage are unobserved for this run by direct artifact evidence.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary contingency. The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared LLM call per paired task). Deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit counts: hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 120, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false.

Primary contingency and statistical summaries. The analysis contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0; the paired difference A − B = 0.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI was computed with bootstrap_resamples = 10,000 and bootstrap_seed = 1729 (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) and returned [0.00, 0.00]. The exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. These statistics are deterministic given the observed degenerate contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv).

Representative per‑task diagnostics showing why repairs were not triggered. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs from the archived bundle directly show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and repair_applied == false for typical tasks: (1) execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false; (2) execution/scoring/task-000002-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 2, required_command_count = 2, validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false; (3) execution/scoring/task-000003-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 6, required_command_count = 6, validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false. These concrete per‑task fields explain mechanistically why the repair path was not invoked: the shared LLM candidates satisfied the validator's required command presence and ordering checks, so no repair invocation was required or recorded. The per‑task JSON artifacts are archived in execution/scoring/*.json and were used directly by the analysis executor.

Contamination and missingness diagnostics. The preregistered contamination checks produced no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty) and missingness diagnostics report complete_pairs = 120 with zero failed or unscorable episodes (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider audit and execution logs show no retries or infrastructure failures beyond the planned single generation per pair; execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json contain the machine‑readable accounting.
sections.discussion:
Measured estimand and scope. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics were used, the executed confirmatory estimand reduces to validator‑acceptance parity: given identical LLM candidates, do downstream orchestration and verification paths differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The observed complete concordance (n11 = 120) answers this restricted question: both validator/orchestrator stacks accepted the identical candidates for every paired task. The run does not exercise independent generator variance, sampling effects, or repair efficacy; consequently preregistered hypotheses about independent generation (H1) and repair coverage (H2) remain preregistered but unobserved under the shared_candidate execution semantics. We explicitly label H1/H2 as unobserved in the Evidence→Claim table and in the Abstract/Introduction.

Artifact‑grounded explanation for concordance. The archival traces explain why concordance occurred: representative scoring JSONs show shared_initial_candidate normalized to include all required commands and ordering constraints (parsed_command_count == required_command_count), producing validation_after.valid == true and repair_applied == false. The task manifest entries include canonical required_sequence and reference_answer fields; provider_call artifacts record that prompts delivered to the model contained only the task intent and constraints (not the canonical reference answer) and that execution isolation prevented prompt/response leakage across conditions (execution/provider_calls/* and execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

Design consequences and recommendations for discriminating follow‑ups. To test the original H1/H2 claims about independent generation and repair performance, follow‑ups should (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair (this increases initial model_calls_used from 120 to 240 as anticipated in the preregistration), (ii) enable independent sampling (multiple initial candidates per arm) to estimate generator variance, and (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied records become observable. Each modification produces distinct archived signatures (higher hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_applied flags, model_calls_used > 120) in the execution and analysis manifests; the preregistration documents these resource and instrumentation tradeoffs.

Threats to validity and operational interpretation. Internal validity: the shared_candidate design intentionally removed generator variance and thus is internally consistent for the validator‑parity estimand; it is not a defect but a narrowing of scope. Construct validity: the binary deterministic validator acceptance is a conservative production gate; richer per‑task parsed counts and violation_codes in the archive enable graded or partial correctness analyses if desired. External validity: the synthetic Mininet‑derived corpus, single model (gpt‑5‑mini), and single deterministic validator limit generality; these constraints are explicit in the preregistration and the Limitations section. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency yields a point mass CI and p = 1.0 and is correctly reported with bootstrap parameters (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Reproducibility and artifact access. All per‑task prompts, responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle (execution/provider_calls/, execution/responses/, execution/scoring/, analysis/). Representative artifact paths are cited throughout this paper and the bundling manifest is recorded in the execution manifest. Interested readers and auditors can inspect the provider_call files (execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, etc.) and per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) to verify the exact prompts sent, the shared candidate delivered, and the validator decisions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifactized paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage are therefore unobserved. The run precisely measures validator‑acceptance parity under controlled shared candidates, provides the archived artifacts that rule out prompt leakage into model prompts (provider_call artifacts and task manifests), and documents the concrete protocol modifications needed to obtain a discriminating comparison that exercises independent generation and repair coverage.

Deterministic artifacts included deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). The run deliberately used the preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: both pipeline arms received the same initial LLM candidate per task; execution accounting shows model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) while planned episodes were 240. Primary analysis used paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Repair was available per the preregistration (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but not triggered: per‑task scoring traces report repair_applied = false and repair_provider_trace_path = null for all episodes (execution/scoring/*.json). Provider_call artifacts record the exact prompts sent to the hosted model for each shared generation (see execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000002-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000003-shared-initial.json) and, together with the task manifest entries (execution/task_manifest.jsonl), demonstrate that prompts contained the task intent and constraints but did not include the canonical reference answers used by the deterministic validator. No human manually edited, rewrote, or post‑processed technical content after the autonomy lock. The Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; the autonomous run performed literature review, final research‑question selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, and manuscript drafting after the lock. Immutable reference to the initial master prompt: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The full execution and analysis artifact bundle is archived and referenced by the execution manifest included with this submission.
limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
